title: Upcountry Community Meeting on Hazard Mitigation & Recovery: February 29, 2024

issues.title: Kula burn scar fencing and native replanting
State fire code adoption with brush clearing fines

recap.headline: Upcountry meeting on wildfire prevention, Firewise and Kula burn scar recovery
recap.in_60_seconds: Council Vice Chair Yuki Lei Sugimura held an Upcountry community meeting on hazard mitigation and recovery after the August 2023 wildfires. The new Maui Emergency Management Agency administrator, the Maui fire chief, Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization and the Kula Community Watershed Alliance presented, and six community members spoke in the question period. Speakers urged neighborhoods to join the Firewise program and explained brush code enforcement, new Upcountry fire equipment, and native replanting of the Kula burn scar. The Alliance said $2.7 million in federal erosion-control money for Kula has been set aside since November but work has not started. Concerns about absentee landowners with overgrown land, green waste drop-off, agricultural burn smoke, burnout and mental health were raised, and most got no firm commitment.

parts.title: Welcome and purpose of the meeting
presented: Upcountry debris removal is complete, and the community is moving into rebuilding and prevention.
Permits normally take about 300 days, and the County passed a bill to speed permits for wildfire victims; her office offers help with rebuild permits.
FEMA staff attended to hear concerns for a hazard mitigation grant that will come through the State.
The Kula Community Watershed Alliance was recently awarded almost $500,000 by the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation.

parts.title: Maui Emergency Management Agency plans
presented: He became administrator on January 1, 2024, after 32 years as a firefighter.
He is proposing six new agency positions, four of which may be grant funded, including a public affairs officer.
The agency strategic plan is almost complete, and a plan to build an incident management team is complete.
West Maui community aid after the fire ran 32 days; with prior preparation he estimated it could have been about 10, so the agency will use the State HI-HARD community preparedness program.

parts.title: Fire department update
presented: The fire code requires vegetation within 30 feet of a structure to be 18 inches or shorter; owners get a 30-day warning, then a violation with fines and another 30 days, after which the department can hire clearing.
Requests to the Fire Prevention Bureau have grown about twentyfold; the Kula inspector has 40 to 50 pending requests.
Kula has a new pumper engine, a funded tanker and an upgraded off-road vehicle; Makawao station is getting a second bay, and this year's budget asks for a wildland truck.
The county has about four Firewise communities, and the community wildfire protection plan update will be led by Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization.

next.what: Public meetings on the community wildfire protection plan update

parts.title: Wildfire trends and the Firewise program
presented: 99% of Hawaiʻi wildfires are caused by people, and about 75% are accidental.
A national model rates Kula at higher wildfire risk than 86% of U.S. communities.
Hawaiʻi had about 12 to 14 Firewise communities before August and now has 30, out of 2,400 nationally, with over 100 resident leaders.
Neighborhoods set their own boundaries, get a walk-around assessment, make an action plan and can earn national recognition that opens extra funding.

parts.title: Kula Community Watershed Alliance burn scar work
presented: Most of what burned in Kula was a 200-acre unmanaged black wattle forest, and it had the highest soil burn severity of the August 8 fires.
The Alliance's four steps are stabilize, protect with fencing, restore with native plants and shaded fuel breaks, and maintain; about 8 acres have been stabilized so far.
The new grant covers about 25 acres plus a community greenhouse and seed banking.
USDA's Emergency Watershed Protection program set aside $2.7 million for Kula erosion control, but it is still in paperwork between the State Attorney General and the local fiscal sponsor.

raised.concern: Federal emergency erosion-control money for Kula, announced in November, has not reached the ground after a full winter.
Firefighters ran out of water because Upcountry water pumps depend on electric power.

next.what: Alliance's first native planting with Kula fire survivors
Soil and water conservation district community meeting on the federal erosion work

raised.concern: The community does the work quickly; funding should go directly to community groups to fix a bottleneck between planning, funding and implementation.
Absentee landowners, plus some County and State parcels, leave large overgrown wattle areas that threaten neighbors, and neighbors cannot get permission to clear them.
There are no green waste drop-off sites Upcountry; residents must haul to Kahului, and a volunteer group pays about $700 per roll-off bin.
With volunteers burned out and resources short at every level, what can families realistically expect from government, including FEMA, in the next fire?
A neighbor's agricultural burn on a windy day sent smoke into a home next to the burn zone, and calls bounced between 911, the Department of Health and the fire department.
Emergency management should plan for community mental health, not only one-on-one counseling.

answered.said: Even emergency funds can take years; her group has waited up to 10 years on some, so communities should act where they can while systems catch up.
Preparation starts at home; only about 15 to 20% of the room had two weeks of supplies.
Preparedness starts with families and helping neighbors; he admitted he does not have 14 days of food stored either.
Nobody is coming to save us; knowing your neighbors is the best defense.
He is looking for the gap in coordinating funding and plans to connect better with the community on grant-funded hazard mitigation projects.
Burnout is real; these are complex problems with fixes on different time scales.
The Department of Health issues agricultural burn permits and prefers windy days; report it to the Department of Health, which can act if a burn becomes a nuisance.

Without a fire code violation within 30 feet of a structure the department cannot enforce; it would take new law, and over 40 fire-related bills are at the State Legislature this year versus 6 to 10 normally.

next.what: Staff will take down unanswered questions and pass them to agencies for answers

parts.title: Closing and sign-ups
presented: Attendees were asked to sign up at the back desk so the office can follow up on participation.
Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization has a Firewise sign-up list and two trained community ambassadors doing home assessments locally.

next.what: County Council Budget Committee visit to hear community priorities

bills.name: County permit bill for wildfire victims
bills.what: Sets up faster permit processing for people rebuilding after the wildfires.

bills.name: Maui Hazard Mitigation Plan
bills.what: Outlines Maui's hazard risks and the government resources available to address them.

bills.name: Maui fire code brush rules
bills.what: Requires vegetation within 30 feet of a structure to be 18 inches or shorter, with warnings, fines and County clearing for violators.

bills.name: Community wildfire protection plan
bills.what: Area wildfire plan to be updated by Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization with public meetings.

open_questions.question: When will the $2.7 million federal Emergency Watershed Protection erosion work in Kula begin?
How will Upcountry water pumps keep running for firefighting when power is out?
Will the County add green waste drop-off sites Upcountry?
What can neighbors do about overgrown absentee-owned or government land that is outside fire code reach?
How is emergency management planning for community mental health after disasters?

not_on_tracker.topic: Delayed federal emergency erosion-control funds for Kula
not_on_tracker.why: Burned slopes and debris-filled gulches stayed unprotected through winter, raising flood and erosion risk.
Neighbors who maintain their own property still face fire risk from large unmanaged wattle stands they cannot clear.
Residents clearing fire fuels must haul to Kahului or pay for private bins.

not_on_tracker.topic: Agricultural burning near the burn zone
not_on_tracker.why: Smoke affects neighbors' health and stress, and they do not know which agency to call.
Volunteer groups doing recovery work say they move faster than agencies but run on donations.

not_on_tracker.topic: Community mental health in disaster planning
not_on_tracker.why: Burnout and trauma are widespread, and many people do not use one-on-one counseling.

moments.quote: The main thing to note is that anything 30 feet from a structure has to be 18 inches or shorter.
moments.about: The fire chief explains the brush clearing standard that the fire code enforces around structures.

moments.quote: The way the process works is if we identify a fire code violation, we will give the owner of the property a notice of warning. They have 30 days to correct it. After that, we give them a notice of violation, which means they're going to be getting fined, and then they have 30 days to correct it.
moments.about: The fire chief lays out the warning, fine and clearing steps the department uses for brush code violations.

moments.quote: And we're going up to collect, we're propagating the seeds, and we're getting ready to have our first planting late next month.
moments.about: The Alliance gives its timeline: native seeds are being collected and propagated, and the first planting on the burn scar is set for late the following month.

moments.quote: We just received a grant, as Yuki Lei mentioned. Part of that grant is going to include a community greenhouse, so that we can actually grow our own and kind of build community around that and educate around that. It also includes stabilization, fencing, planting, and you know...
moments.about: The Alliance explains that its new grant pays for a community greenhouse, stabilization, fencing and planting on about 25 acres of the Kula burn scar.

moments.quote: We went through the entire winter without anything, except for what we could do ourselves. To me, that's unacceptable.
moments.about: The Alliance describes the community waiting since November for $2.7 million in federal emergency watershed erosion-control work on the Kula burn area.

moments.quote: But remember, the fire code is 30 feet from the nearest structure. And so a lot of people are protected from that, but we have to change legislation, which we may see some of that this year.
moments.about: The fire chief says the current code's 30-foot limit leaves overgrown absentee parcels outside enforcement, so the rules would have to change to reach them.
